papers.title: AALS SECTION ON CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL SCHOLARSHIP: WHAT SHOULD WE STUDY AND HOW SHOULD WE STUDY IT?: An Empirical Study of Securities Disclosure Practice
papers.authors: Stephen J. Choi* and G. Mitu Gulati +
papers.abstract:
How are decisions on what information to disclose and what not to disclose in securities offering documents made? One can imagine lawyers advising their clients on how to comply with the law, especially while facing ambiguous legal mandates. In our imagined scenario, lawyers wrestle with the legal detail in arriving at a reasoned conclusion on whether a particular piece of new information must be disclosed in offering documents. But does our imagined scenario match reality? Is this really how securities lawyers tackle disclosure questions in the course of their transactional practices? This Article looks at how sovereign issuers and their lawyers change their disclosure practices in securities offering documents in response to material changes in the substantive allocation of rights in the underlying sovereign debt contract terms.
One view is that material changes are swiftly and clearly spelled out in new offering documents. Sophisticated attorneys and their clients pay close attention to any change that may affect what the law requires them to disclose and alter their disclosure accordingly. We call this the "Legal Compliance" view. Conversely, disclosure practices may suffer from network effects, leading to "stickiness" in what is disclosed even in the face of material changes in the underlying meaning of the disclosure language. Rather than engage in the costly and uncertain effort of determining whether disclosure isrequired under the federal securities laws, attorneys may look to the market standard disclosure practices as an indicator of the required disclosures. Once a particular disclosure practice becomes standard, deviation from this standard may send a negative signal to the marketplace and, thereby, reduce investor interest in the offering. Issuers and their attorneys may also hesitate to change existing disclosure practices out of a desire to influence how the market and courts interpret the contract. We refer to this as the "Network Stickiness" view. This Article tests between the Legal Compliance and Network Stickiness views of securities disclosure practices.
Focusing on the sovereign debt market cabins our inquiry in a manner that allows us to say something about a specific set of lawyers engaged in a particular type of transactional practice. The sovereign debt market consists of some of the most sophisticated and expensive lawyers in the world, engaged in routine but large transactions (at a minimum, in the hundreds of millions of dollars). It is precisely in the sovereign bond market where we expect issuers and their attorneys to have the expertise and inclination to focus on securities disclosure issues. Contrary to expectation, we provide preliminary evidence in this Article that disclosure practices are sticky even in the face of material changes to the meaning of boilerplate terms.
For our analysis, we examine sovereign bond offerings from 1985 to 2005. We restrict our sample to include a selection of major issuers in terms of deal volume (Mexico, Brazil, and Colombia) and a set of issuers drawn from geographically diverse regions (Italy, China, Philippines, Lebanon, Israel, Jamaica, and South Africa). The sample consists primarily of shelf registration offerings with a limited number of private placements.
Our tests focus on the disclosures sovereign issuers made in prospectus supplements (in the registered offering context) and offering circulars (in the private placement context). We examine the disclosure response of issuers (and their attorneys) for three major shifts in the underlying substance of the sovereign bond contracts governing the bonds issued in the shelf registration offerings. Two of the shifts involve unexpected changes in interpretations of existing contractual language: the "Exit Consent" innovation and the Pari Passu shock. The third shift involved an explicit change in the actual contract language: the move toward collective action clauses (CACs) from unanimity action clauses (UACs) for changes to payment-related terms. This third shift, in contrast to the first two shifts, had beenextensively vetted prior to the shift by market participants, the official sector, and academic researchers.
The difference between the first two shifts, involving changes in the interpretation of existing contract terms, and the third shift, involving a change in the explicit contract term, allows us to examine when issuers and their lawyers are more likely to disclose changes in the underlying substantive allocation of rights in the contract. While all three shifts change the substantive allocation of rights, we hypothesize that issuers and their lawyers are more likely to disclose changes that occur, not through a change in the interpretation of the existing boilerplate language, but rather, through explicit change in the language itself. Because explicit language changes are more obvious, and thus nondisclosure more easily noticed by investors and potential plaintiffs' attorneys, the issuer and its attorneys face greater costs from failure to disclose the contractual changes as part of the offering documentation.Conversely, disclosing a change due to a shift in contractual interpretation may have the negative effect, particularly when the interpretive shift is somewhat uncertain, of solidifying a particular, and from the issuer's perspective, unfavorable interpretation. Alternatively, attorneys pressed for time in a rapidly moving shelf takedown offering may expend only limited resources in searching for possible required disclosures, leading the attorneys to focus disproportionately on obvious, easily observable changes in the substantive contractual rights (for example, an explicit change in the contract language) and too little attention on changes due to external causes, such as an interpretive shock (the "rule of thumb" approach to disclosure).
Part II describes the three major shifts in the underlying substantive allocations of rights that occurred in the sovereign debt market for issuances governed under New York law in the early 2000s. Part III discusses the legal duty under U.S. securities regulations placed on issuers to disclose information on these shifts in the prospectus supplement as part of a shelf registration sale of securities. Part IV sets out our hypotheses and Part V describes the data, countryby country. Part VI matches the hypotheses against the data and Part VII concludes.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries, disclosure practices, and creditor composition (activist vs passive, domestic vs foreign) affect bargaining, pricing, and restructuring trajectories?
matches.specific_contribution: Using sovereign offering documents from 1985–2005, the study tests whether disclosure adjusts to interpretive shocks (exit consents, pari passu) versus explicit clause rewrites (shift to CACs) and presents preliminary evidence that disclosure practices remain sticky even when boilerplate meaning materially changes, consistent with signaling and network effects.
matches.generalized_contribution: Sticky disclosure practices can impede transmission of information about material shifts in creditor rights, with implications for pricing and bargaining in sovereign debt.
matches.research_idea: Collect and code sovereign offering documents around interpretive shocks (exit consents, pari passu) and explicit clause changes (CAC adoption) to test whether disclosure adjustments differ across these events and whether stickiness correlates with proxies for investor demand at issuance.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do legal ambiguities and doctrinal vagueness (e.g., in 'pari passu', 'loan' definitions, or damages measures) cause litigation, market uncertainty, and suboptimal contracting outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on sovereign offerings from 1985–2005, the study hypothesizes and tests that ambiguity from interpretive shocks to boilerplate (exit consents, pari passu) suppresses disclosure of the resulting rights shifts—partly to avoid cementing unfavorable readings—whereas explicit clause changes are more likely to be disclosed; it presents preliminary evidence of overall disclosure stickiness despite material changes.
matches.generalized_contribution: Legal ambiguity surrounding boilerplate can depress issuer disclosure of material shifts in rights, producing sticky and potentially suboptimal contracting disclosures even when obligations meaningfully change.
matches.research_idea: Empirically test whether interpretive shocks to boilerplate clauses versus explicit rewrites change the incidence and detail of disclosures in sovereign offering documents by constructing a panel of issuances and coding disclosure content before and after each shock.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries-adverse selection and moral hazard-shape the design of contractual devices (collateral, covenants, disclosure) in sovereign and corporate lending?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a hand-collected dataset of sovereign bond offering documents from 1985–2005 across major issuers, the study tests disclosure responses to three material shifts in contractual rights (exit consents, the pari passu shock, and CAC adoption) and presents preliminary evidence that disclosures are sticky and more responsive to explicit language changes than to interpretive shifts, reflecting network and signaling considerations over pure legal compliance.
matches.generalized_contribution: In sophisticated debt markets, disclosure practices can be path-dependent and more reactive to obvious textual revisions than to interpretive changes, shaped by network effects and signaling concerns rather than solely by legal mandates.
matches.research_idea: Collect a panel of sovereign offering prospectuses and test whether disclosures about material shifts in creditor rights track explicit clause rewrites more than interpretive shocks, to assess the role of signaling and network effects in disclosure design.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do information asymmetries and signaling affect creditor decision-making and pricing in sovereign and complex financial contracting?
matches.specific_contribution: The Network Stickiness account posits that deviating from market-standard disclosure may send a negative signal and reduce investor interest, discouraging issuers and counsel from updating disclosures after interpretive shocks.
matches.generalized_contribution: Investor signaling concerns can deter timely updates to disclosures in response to non-textual changes in contractual rights.
matches.research_idea: Using issuance-level pricing or order book data, test whether sovereign offerings with non-standard disclosure language face weaker investor demand or wider spreads than issues that hew to market-standard disclosures.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do standardized boilerplate clauses (e.g., pari passu, governing-law, indemnities) generate systemic litigation externalities and market-wide vulnerabilities?
matches.specific_contribution: By using the pari passu shock and the exit consent innovation—unexpected interpretive shifts in boilerplate—as tests for disclosure responses, the study highlights how standard clauses can undergo abrupt meaning changes with litigation implications that may not be promptly reflected in offering documents.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized boilerplate is vulnerable to sudden interpretive shifts that propagate uncertainty and litigation risk across markets, and disclosure practices may lag in acknowledging these shifts.
matches.research_idea: Assemble prospectuses around major interpretive shocks to boilerplate clauses and measure how quickly and extensively issuers disclose the resulting litigation risks and rights reallocations.

matches.theme_name: Do professional intermediaries (law firms, underwriters, trustees, advisors) introduce agency costs that bias contract design and risk allocation?
matches.specific_contribution: Analyzing sovereign offerings from 1985–2005, the study presents preliminary evidence that even elite transactional lawyers rely on market-standard templates and rule-of-thumb heuristics—especially under time pressure—so disclosures lag material interpretive changes in underlying rights.
matches.generalized_contribution: Professional intermediaries can entrench sticky, suboptimal disclosure practices by following market conventions and low-effort heuristics rather than individualized legal analysis.
matches.research_idea: Track law-firm-specific disclosure language over time around known shifts in contractual rights to test whether firms promptly update drafting or instead mirror prevailing market templates.

matches.theme_name: Are market-based restructuring instruments (debt-equity swaps, exit consents, buybacks) as effective and equitable as formal legal remedies in reallocating burdens during sovereign restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: The exit consent innovation serves as one interpretive shift used to test whether issuers described its effects in offering documents, suggesting such market-based restructuring tools may not be promptly or clearly disclosed.
matches.generalized_contribution: Market-based restructuring mechanisms may not be consistently or promptly highlighted in offering disclosures after their emergence, reflecting disclosure stickiness.
matches.research_idea: Compile and code prospectuses before and after the emergence of exit consents to assess whether and how their mechanics and distributional effects are disclosed.

matches.theme_name: What role do lawyers, underwriters, and other intermediaries play in creating, diffusing, and entrenching contractual innovations and standard clauses?
matches.specific_contribution: Using sovereign bond prospectus supplements and offering circulars from 1985–2005 across major issuers, the study provides preliminary evidence that elite sovereign-debt lawyers follow market-standard templates and keep disclosures sticky even after material interpretive changes (e.g., Exit Consent and Pari Passu shocks), contrasting these with explicit clause changes such as the move from UACs to CACs.
matches.generalized_contribution: Intermediaries’ reliance on standard-form practices entrenches disclosure templates, yielding slow or selective updates in response to changes in the substantive meaning of boilerplate terms.
matches.research_idea: Collect and code sovereign bond offering documents around major contractual shifts (interpretive shocks like Exit Consent and Pari Passu and explicit changes like CAC adoption) to test whether lawyers update disclosures in line with legal compliance expectations or adhere to network-standard templates.

matches.theme_name: How do legal and institutional shocks (financial crises, regime change, pandemics) drive changes in contractual practice and market pricing?
matches.specific_contribution: Analyzing sovereign issuances governed by New York law, the article provides preliminary evidence that interpretive shocks such as the Exit Consent innovation and the Pari Passu reinterpretation did not prompt commensurate disclosure updates, whereas the study contrasts these with an explicit language change—the shift from UACs to CACs—used to gauge when disclosure changes occur.
matches.generalized_contribution: Legal and interpretive shocks reshape contractual practice unevenly: visible textual revisions are more likely to trigger disclosure changes, while interpretive shifts often leave disclosure practices sticky.
matches.research_idea: Use a panel of sovereign bond offering documents spanning interpretive shocks and explicit clause revisions to measure whether and when legal or institutional shocks trigger changes in disclosure practice, and identify the conditions under which such shocks fail to move practice.

matches.theme_name: To what extent does legal indeterminacy and doctrinal vagueness increase transaction costs and reduce cross-border capital flows?
matches.specific_contribution: Using sovereign bond offering documents from 1985–2005 around three major shifts (Exit Consents, the Pari Passu shock, and the move from UACs to CACs), the study provides preliminary evidence that when interpretive shifts are uncertain, issuers and counsel often do not update disclosures—consistent with attorneys avoiding costly, ambiguous determinations and relying on rule-of-thumb focus on obvious textual changes.
matches.generalized_contribution: Legal indeterminacy in interpretive developments induces market participants to avoid costly evaluation and to under-adjust disclosures relative to explicit rule changes.
matches.research_idea: Measure how disclosure revision rates differ after interpretive shocks versus explicit contractual amendments in sovereign bonds, using a panel of offering documents to infer the transaction-cost impact of legal indeterminacy.

matches.theme_name: How does judicial interpretive flexibility (vague standards vs precise rules) affect predictability and market behavior in high-stakes transactional and sovereign debt litigation?
matches.specific_contribution: Examining sovereign offerings from 1985–2005, the study finds that issuers and their lawyers more consistently disclose explicit changes to contract language (such as adoption of CACs) than shifts in the interpretation of boilerplate terms (Exit Consents and Pari Passu), yielding sticky disclosure practices in the face of interpretive uncertainty.
matches.generalized_contribution: Market participants adjust disclosures more readily to precise textual rule changes than to flexible or uncertain interpretive developments, affecting predictability and the timing of behavioral responses.
matches.research_idea: Compare disclosure updates in sovereign offering documents following explicit contractual amendments versus interpretive shocks to assess how rule precision versus interpretive flexibility shapes market-facing disclosures.

matches.theme_name: Do lawyers, deal teams, and legal intermediaries (as repeat players) add measurable economic value through drafting and structuring beyond mere documentation?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a dataset of sovereign bond offering documents spanning 1985–2005, the study provides preliminary evidence that even elite sovereign debt counsel tend to follow market-standard, sticky disclosure templates and update them primarily when language changes are explicit rather than when substantive rights shift via interpretive developments.
matches.generalized_contribution: Legal intermediaries in high-stakes transactions often default to market-standard disclosures and respond more to visible textual changes than to interpretive shifts, limiting tailored, value-adding adjustments in disclosure design.
matches.research_idea: Assemble a cross-country panel of sovereign offering documents around known contractual and interpretive shifts and test whether elite counsel tailor disclosures to substantive legal changes or adhere to network-standard language.

matches.theme_name: To what degree do soft-law norms, reputation, and market practice substitute for enforceable legal remedies in cross-border finance?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a corpus of sovereign bond prospectus supplements and offering circulars from major issuers (1985–2005) around three contractual shifts, the study provides preliminary evidence that disclosure practices are sticky and track market-standard templates rather than adjusting to material shifts in underlying rights, consistent with reputational and network-effects constraints on counsel.
matches.generalized_contribution: In cross-border securities offerings, market practice and reputational signals can outweigh formal legal changes in driving disclosure behavior.
matches.research_idea: Assemble and code a longitudinal corpus of sovereign bond offering documents around known contractual and interpretive shifts, and test whether disclosure updates follow prevailing market-standard language rather than the timing or substance of the shifts, to gauge the disciplining role of soft-law norms.

matches.theme_name: What can large-scale, contract-by-contract textual and empirical analyses reveal about the gap between drafted language and actual functional allocations of risk?
matches.specific_contribution: Comparing disclosure responses to two interpretive shocks (Exit Consents and Pari Passu) versus an explicit textual change (shift to CACs) in a 1985–2005 sovereign bond corpus, the study finds preliminary evidence that disclosures often fail to reflect functional shifts in rights when those shifts stem from interpretation rather than from revised contract text.
matches.generalized_contribution: Systematic corpus analysis can reveal gaps where disclosures and boilerplate drafting lag actual functional reallocations of rights, especially when those reallocations arise from interpretive rather than textual change.
matches.research_idea: Build and code a contract-by-contract corpus of sovereign offering documents across interpretive and textual shocks, and test whether disclosures track only explicit textual revisions, thereby identifying gaps between written terms and functional rights.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do judicial interpretations of boilerplate contractual language shape market practice and subsequent contract drafting?

matches.research_idea: Compile timelines of major judicial or interpretive shifts affecting sovereign bond boilerplate and empirically test whether and when issuers revise offering disclosures in response across a coded document corpus.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries, signaling, and hidden actors shape representations, warranties, and verification clauses in high-value cross-border contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: The introduction posits that departing from market-standard disclosure language can send a negative signal to investors, discouraging issuers and counsel from updating disclosures even when underlying contractual rights change.
matches.generalized_contribution: Signaling concerns can entrench standard-form disclosures in high-value cross-border offerings despite informational changes.
matches.research_idea: Empirically code deviations from market-standard disclosure language in a corpus of cross-border sovereign offerings and test whether updates cluster only after the market standard itself shifts, consistent with signaling-driven stickiness.

matches.theme_name: How do agency problems among intermediaries (banks, law firms, underwriters, trustees) distort contract terms and affect post-signing enforcement and renegotiation outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: Using sovereign bond prospectus supplements and offering circulars from 1985–2005 across major issuers, the study presents preliminary evidence that issuers and their lawyers follow market-standard disclosure even after material interpretive shifts (e.g., exit consents, pari passu), while they more readily update disclosure after explicit clause changes (e.g., CAC adoption), consistent with signaling concerns, litigation risk, and time-pressured rule-of-thumb review.

matches.theme_name: How do domestic courts, international arbitration, and official institutions (e.g., IMF) interact to determine bargaining leverage and the legality of restructuring plans?
matches.specific_contribution: Analyzing sovereign bond disclosures around the exit-consent innovation, the pari passu shock, and the CAC shift, the study suggests issuers and their lawyers are less likely to disclose changes arising from judicial reinterpretations—partly to avoid solidifying unfavorable readings—than changes from explicit contract amendments, which are more visibly disclosed.
matches.generalized_contribution: When courts reframe the meaning of contract terms, issuers may strategically limit disclosure to avoid entrenching adverse interpretations, whereas explicit amendments elicit clearer disclosure.
matches.research_idea: Compare disclosure behavior in sovereign offerings following court-driven interpretive shocks versus explicit contract amendments to test whether concerns about cementing adverse judicial interpretations suppress issuer disclosure that could influence future adjudication.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a hand-collected dataset of sovereign bond offering documents from 1985–2005 across major issuers, the study tests a Legal Compliance versus Network Stickiness account and provides preliminary evidence that disclosure practices are sticky and change more when clause text is explicitly revised (e.g., CAC adoption) than when meaning shifts through interpretation (exit consents, pari passu), consistent with network effects, signaling concerns, and time-pressured rule-of-thumb lawyering.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized disclosure practices in sophisticated debt markets persist due to network effects and signaling costs, adjusting more readily to visible textual revisions than to interpretive shifts.
matches.research_idea: Collect and analyze a cross-issuer dataset of sovereign offering documents to test whether market-standard disclosure language persists after material shifts in the meaning of boilerplate terms and whether changes occur more often when the clause text is explicitly revised than when interpretations shift.

matches.theme_name: Can empirical contract-level datasets reveal patterns of clause prevalence and evolution that should inform doctrinal or regulatory reform?
matches.specific_contribution: By assembling prospectus supplements and offering circulars for sovereign bond offerings (1985–2005) and coding disclosures around exit consents, pari passu, and the CAC shift, the study reveals patterned, sticky disclosure responses to contract-rights shocks.
matches.generalized_contribution: Empirical corpora of contracts and offering documents can uncover systematic, sticky responses to shifts in contractual rights that doctrinal narratives alone may miss.

matches.theme_name: Do legal-opinion practices and interpretive uncertainty among advisors increase transaction costs and systematically shape how contracts are drafted and priced?

matches.generalized_contribution: Interpretive uncertainty and opinion-risk among transactional lawyers promote conservative, standardized drafting choices that downplay contested interpretive shifts in favor of obvious textual changes.
matches.research_idea: Empirically assess whether interpretive uncertainty and time constraints correlate with reliance on standard disclosure language and limited discussion of contested interpretive shifts in sovereign offering documents.

matches.theme_name: How do norms, professional networks, and market practice diffuse contractual innovations (like new clause language) across jurisdictions and market segments?

matches.generalized_contribution: Professional networks and prevailing market practices influence the visibility and diffusion of contractual innovations, with broadly vetted text-based changes more readily propagated in disclosures than subtler interpretive shifts.
matches.research_idea: Trace disclosure of clause innovations across sovereign issuers and jurisdictions to test whether prior vetting by market and official-sector networks predicts faster and more consistent disclosure adoption than innovations arising from interpretive shocks.

matches.theme_name: How do secondary markets and market-level standardization affect the diffusion of contract terms, the formation of expectations, and the potential for contagion across financial contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a dataset of sovereign bond offerings from 1985–2005 and tracking prospectus supplements and offering circulars around three major contractual shifts (exit consents, the pari passu interpretation shock, and the move from UACs to CACs), the Article provides preliminary evidence that disclosure practices exhibit network-driven stickiness, with issuers more likely to update disclosures after explicit text changes than after interpretive shifts.
matches.generalized_contribution: Market standardization and network effects sustain disclosure templates even when underlying contractual rights change, making disclosures more responsive to explicit textual revisions than to interpretive shocks.
matches.research_idea: Measure how often sovereign offering disclosures change following explicit clause amendments versus interpretive shocks by assembling prospectus supplements and offering circulars across major issuers and testing whether standardized market practices produce disclosure inertia.

matches.theme_name: How does legal and drafting complexity affect transaction costs, negotiability, and the likelihood of litigation or deal failure?
matches.specific_contribution: The introduction indicates that, faced with ambiguous mandates and time-pressured shelf takedowns, attorneys avoid the costly and uncertain task of reassessing disclosure after interpretive shocks and instead rely on rule-of-thumb updates, prioritizing obvious explicit textual changes because nondisclosure is easily noticed by investors and potential plaintiffs.

matches.research_idea: Empirically compare disclosure updates following interpretive shocks versus explicit textual amendments across sovereign offerings and test whether greater interpretive complexity and time pressure reduce updating and correlate with higher litigation incidence or offering discounts.

matches.theme_name: Do standardized contract forms and drafting defaults systematically shape non-price deal terms and bargaining outcomes?

matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized market disclosure practices and drafting defaults can drive inertia in non-price terms, with updates more likely when changes are made explicit in the text than when they arise from interpretive shifts.
matches.research_idea: Assemble a panel of sovereign offering documents around interpretive shocks and explicit clause amendments to test whether standardized templates cause disclosure inertia, with greater updating when contract language changes than when interpretations shift.

matches.theme_name: How does the degree of clause specificity (precise proxies vs vague standards) in contracts affect ex-post renegotiation costs, adaptability to shocks, and judicial interpretation?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a dataset of sovereign bond offerings from 1985–2005 around three contractual shocks (exit consents, pari passu, and the move to CACs), the study provides preliminary evidence that issuers and counsel adjust disclosures more in response to explicit language changes than to interpretive shifts, likely because explicit changes are more visible and create clearer nondisclosure risk.
matches.generalized_contribution: Explicit contractual revisions elicit more responsive disclosure behavior than interpretive shifts, as visibility and enforcement risk make parties more likely to update disclosures when language, rather than interpretation, changes.
matches.research_idea: Compare disclosure adjustments following explicit textual amendments versus interpretive shocks in sovereign bond contracts by constructing an issuer-level panel of offering documents around each shock and testing differential responsiveness.

matches.theme_name: When do private ordering and standardized boilerplate generate negative externalities for third parties that warrant public-policy or regulatory intervention?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on sovereign bond disclosure records from 1985–2005, the study offers preliminary evidence that network effects and signaling concerns make disclosure practices sticky even after material shifts in contractual rights, suggesting that market-standard boilerplate can impede timely, informative updates for investors.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized private-ordering practices in disclosure can persist despite material contractual changes, creating information gaps for investors and potential negative externalities beyond the contracting parties.
matches.research_idea: Assemble a cross-issuer, multi-year dataset of sovereign offering documents around known contractual or interpretive shocks and test whether market-standard disclosure language persists despite material rights changes, indicating externalities that could justify regulatory intervention.

matches.theme_name: What are the trade-offs between standardized boilerplate and bespoke drafting for transaction costs, liquidity, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: Using disclosures in prospectus supplements and offering circulars from 1985–2005 across major sovereign issuers, the study provides preliminary evidence that disclosure practices are sticky and are updated more when contract text changes explicitly (e.g., the shift from UACs to CACs) than when substantive meaning shifts through interpretive shocks (exit consents and the pari passu episode).

matches.research_idea: Assemble a dataset of sovereign bond prospectus supplements and offering circulars across major issuers and test whether disclosure updates track explicit changes in contract text more than interpretive shocks, thereby distinguishing legal-compliance behavior from network stickiness.

papers.title: ARTICLE: THE DYNAMICS OF CONTRACT EVOLUTION
papers.authors: Stephen J. Choi,* Mitu Gulati+ and Eric A. Posner++
papers.abstract:
The literature on the evolution or production of contracts is sparse. Scholars frequently assume that parties draft bespoke contracts that serve the needs of specific transactions.But this assumption does not reflect the reality of the contract production process.
Contracts are more like commodities than custom-made items. They are mass-produced by law firms, which typically serve large numbers of clients with divergent interests.Like any other mass producer seeking to serve a broad client base, law firms sell products that help serve the needs of clients. The client typically wishes to consummatea deal - not to produce the perfect contract.The economics of the production process then results in a method where lawyers produce "good enough" contracts, and where the majority of these contracts are modifications of existing templates, including older contracts or forms that have been developed by trade associations.
Barak Richman explains that "the paradigmatic question each attorney asks regarding a new legal product is, 'Has this worked before?' not 'How can we make this work best?' or even 'What is it that we are making?'"Contract drafters are more like inventors than authors: They take existing products and try to improve them so that they can meet the clients' needs at hand. As a result, contract production is path-dependent, giving rise to the phenomenon of boilerplate.Boilerplate has an odd dual quality: It is thought to be necessary (which is why it is left in the contract), but parties often do not know why it is important. Judicial opinions reflect this confusion, with many courts expressing skepticism about boilerplate even while they frequently enforce it.
Boilerplate is sticky but not static. We know that boilerplate and form contracts generally change over time. But we know little about how these contracts change. In a prior article, we examined the evolution of sovereign debt contracts over a roughly fifty-year period.We found that changes did not occur on a deal-to-deal basis as assumed by the conventional model. Rather, contracts generally changed on an industry-wide basis, in response to major events, such as global financial crises.Individualized change also tended to show up in response to shocks or significant events, but the events in question were significantfor particular actors and not the market as a whole. In the case of sovereign debtors, individual defaults, rather than regional or global crises, provide the spark to alter boilerplate and form contracts.
In this article, we extend our prior research to analyze the internal dynamics of these periods of clustered change and assess how boilerplate terms shift to a new standard. The industry we use in our analysis is the sovereign bond market for foreign-law governed bonds. These bonds are typically purchased by cross-border investors and are largely governed by either the laws of New York or England. The parties in this market - such as states, banks, mutual funds, pension funds, and hedge funds - tend to be sophisticated. Regulation is sparse; after all, the key actors are the states themselves. The basic economic problem in the transaction has remained the same over centuries: States borrow money from foreign investors, but it is hard to force the states to pay the money back if the states decide they would rather not. States nonetheless have an economic incentive to give investors some confidence in getting repaid in order to convince the investors to lend to the states in the first place. The stability of this basic economic transaction over time is important because it enables us to test our evolutionary model over a long period of time.
We focus on a particular shift in the boilerplate sovereign bond contract for those issuances governed under New York law: the shift toward collective action clauses (or "CACs") from unanimity action clauses (or "UACs") governing changes to payment-related terms. The shift to CACs was a watershed event in the history of sovereign bond covenants.It significantly increased the ability of bondholders and issuers to engage in debt restructurings.Our interest is not onlywith how and when New York-law governed contracts shifted from UACs to CACs for payment terms but also the process of change for a number of other CAC-related terms, including the vote threshold for non-payment terms as well as disenfranchisement, mandatory meeting, and aggregation clauses (we define these later). Together, particular combinations of these terms form the model that applies in any particular sovereign bond contract. In discussing the evolution of this model, we will occasionally describe innovations as major and minor. Consistent with the policy debates over CACs, we label the shift away from the requirement of unanimous approval from all bondholders to alter payment terms as the major shift and the changes in other terms as minor shifts.
Shocks to the sovereign debt market, in the form of Mexico's crisis in 1995, the Asian financial crisis in 1997-1998, and Argentina's default in 2001, represented triggers for the changes in the contract model. We report on the types of contract innovations that took place with the start of these shocks and the market participants associated with these changes. Importantly, a shift towards the CAC model as the new standard did not occur overnight. Instead, there was a period of time after Mexico's crisis in 1995 through Argentina's default in 2001 during which the use of CACs was infrequent and only associated with more marginal market participants.
After this initial period, a tipping point occurred - driven by the cumulative effect of the default shocks as well as vocal public sector pressure - at which point top market participants changed from supporting the old standard to competing actively with one another to generate the new standard. At this tipping point, the usage of the old standard dropped rapidly and the incidence of the new CACs increased dramatically - giving an X pattern at the point where their usage percentages in the market crossed. Our study shows that once this tipping point - the X point - is reached, subsequent CAC innovations, largely involving CAC-related terms such as the aggregationclause, are driven by the top market participants competing to control the new CAC standard. This competition eventually led to a new standard - Mexico's version of the CAC first used in 2003 - and a gradual slowing of growth in the adoption of the CAC model in the market as CACs saturated the market. This slow initial experimentation, then rapid acceleration of adoption, followed lastly by a slower growth rate of market adoption as the CAC became dominant, roughly takes the shape of an S curve.
In Part I, we survey the literature on contract innovation. We draw from this literature to set up our hypotheses regarding the process of boilerplate contract evolution. We also describe our sovereign bond dataset, including the key CAC clauses, and the shocks to the sovereign bond market during the time period of our dataset that we use in our empirical tests. These shocks primarily affected issuers using New York-law governed bonds, and that was the market segment from which the impetus for innovation arose. Part II presents evidence from the New York-law governed portion of our sovereign bond dataset on the process of contract change. Part III extends our analysis to the parallel contractual change that occurred in the CACs within the English-law governed sovereign bond market. We use differences in how contract innovation occurred in this separate market to illuminate what distinguishes the initial stages of contract innovation from later stages of new contract standardization. In particular, the presence of external calls for change (in our case, from the public sector) is an important factor in determining when top market participants shift from defending the existing standard to competing in order to generate the new standard.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a sovereign-bond dataset across New York- and English-law issuances, the study shows that boilerplate persists due to path-dependent, template-driven mass production and that lock-in is overcome when cumulative crisis shocks and public-sector pressure induce top market participants to pivot, triggering a tipping point and S-curve adoption of CACs.
matches.generalized_contribution: Boilerplate persists through path dependence and template economics, and clustered shocks plus public-sector nudges that flip leading market participants can overcome lock-in and rapidly standardize new terms.
matches.research_idea: Assemble a longitudinal sovereign-bond clause dataset across New York- and English-law issuances and test whether crisis shocks and public-sector advocacy precipitate tipping points in which leading issuers and their counsel drive rapid replacement of entrenched boilerplate.

matches.theme_name: Do the legal norms and contracting practices centered in major financial hubs (New York, London) produce convergence in sovereign-debt contract terms worldwide, and under what mechanisms?
matches.specific_contribution: Comparing New York- and English-law sovereign bond markets, the study documents parallel shifts toward CACs and shows that external public-sector calls for change influenced when top market participants in each hub moved from defending the old standard to competing to set the new one, promoting standardization toward CACs.
matches.generalized_contribution: Dominant New York- and London-centered markets can generate convergence in sovereign-debt boilerplate when public-sector pressure induces elite participants to coordinate on a new standard.
matches.research_idea: Compare clause-evolution timelines in New York- and English-law sovereign bonds to test whether and how public-sector advocacy and elite market participants in each hub drive convergence toward common CAC terms.

matches.theme_name: What role do lawyers, underwriters, and other intermediaries play in creating, diffusing, and entrenching contractual innovations and standard clauses?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a sovereign-bond contract dataset spanning the UAC-to-CAC transition, the study finds that early innovations were confined to marginal actors, after which leading issuers and their counsel competed to shape and diffuse the new CAC standard (including related terms like aggregation) once a tipping point was reached.
matches.generalized_contribution: Elite market participants and their lawyers originate, refine, and entrench contractual innovations, with diffusion accelerating when top players compete to define the standard.
matches.research_idea: Map clause innovations to specific issuers and counsel across sovereign issuances and estimate whether adoption accelerates once leading participants begin incorporating the new terms.

matches.theme_name: Can empirical contract-level datasets reveal patterns of clause prevalence and evolution that should inform doctrinal or regulatory reform?
matches.specific_contribution: Drawing on a sovereign-bond dataset covering multiple crises and jurisdictions, the study uncovers S-curve adoption dynamics, tipping points, and the sequencing of CAC-related terms, illustrating how contract-level data can reveal patterns relevant to policy debates over boilerplate reform.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contract-level datasets can identify systematic patterns in boilerplate evolution—including tipping points and diffusion paths—that inform doctrinal and regulatory interventions.
matches.research_idea: Build and analyze a multi-jurisdiction contract corpus to detect diffusion curves and co-movement in boilerplate terms around shocks, and draw implications for targeted regulatory nudges.

matches.theme_name: How do legal and institutional shocks (financial crises, regime change, pandemics) drive changes in contractual practice and market pricing?
matches.specific_contribution: Using evidence from a sovereign-bond dataset, the study shows that financial crises (Mexico 1995, Asia 1997–98) and Argentina’s 2001 default triggered initial, marginal adoption of CACs, and that cumulative shocks plus public-sector pressure produced a tipping point after which CAC use surged and later stabilized in an S-curve.
matches.generalized_contribution: Legal and financial shocks catalyze contractual change by initiating experimentation among fringe actors and, with sustained pressure, induce rapid market-wide adoption once a tipping point is crossed.
matches.research_idea: Test whether and when sovereign-debt crises and public-sector advocacy precipitate tipping points in clause adoption by modeling CAC uptake over time across issuance cohorts.

matches.theme_name: How do norms, professional networks, and market practice diffuse contractual innovations (like new clause language) across jurisdictions and market segments?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a longitudinal dataset of sovereign bonds governed by New York and English law, the study documents industry-wide diffusion of CACs triggered by crises and amplified by public-sector advocacy, with early adoption by marginal participants, a tipping-point “X” crossover in usage, and subsequent top-actor competition that produced standardization (e.g., Mexico’s 2003 CAC model) in an S-curve pattern.
matches.generalized_contribution: Contractual innovations in sophisticated markets diffuse via path-dependent, industry-wide S-curve dynamics in which shocks and external advocacy catalyze a shift from marginal experimentation to top-actor competition and standardization across market segments and jurisdictions.
matches.research_idea: Build a longitudinal corpus of New York- and English-law sovereign bonds to map clause-level diffusion and test whether external shocks and public-sector advocacy predict tipping points at which leading intermediaries drive rapid cross-market standardization.

matches.theme_name: Do collective-action clauses (CACs), unanimity clauses (UACs), and related contractual devices reliably prevent holdouts and enable orderly sovereign debt restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: In analyzing the shift from unanimity to collective action clauses in New York–law sovereign bonds, the study reports that CACs significantly increased the ability of bondholders and issuers to conduct restructurings while tracking related features such as aggregation, disenfranchisement, and meeting clauses in its dataset.
matches.generalized_contribution: Collective action mechanisms and related terms in sovereign bond contracts increase the practical capacity to conduct restructurings and mitigate coordination hurdles.

matches.theme_name: Can private ordering, market-level contractual design, and intermediaries substitute effectively for statutory or multilateral interventions in solving cross-border collective-action problems?

matches.theme_name: How do bargaining power asymmetries and repeat-player advantages shape non-price contract terms and the distribution of surplus in sovereign and major corporate transactions?

matches.research_idea: Test whether issues led by top-tier underwriters or frequent sovereign issuers are more likely to introduce and propagate specific CAC features before and after market shocks using deal- and participant-level data.

matches.theme_name: How do market conditions, bargaining power, and counterparty composition drive adoption and specific wording of non-price clauses (MAE/MAC, covenants, break fees) in M&A and lending contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a sovereign bond dataset covering New York- and English-law issuances, the study shows that crisis shocks initially led marginal market participants to adopt CACs and related terms (e.g., vote thresholds, aggregation, disenfranchisement), and that a tipping point—driven by cumulative defaults and vocal public-sector pressure—prompted top market participants to compete to define and diffuse the new standard.
matches.generalized_contribution: Clause adoption and wording in sophisticated debt markets are shaped by crisis shocks, the status of market participants, and external policy pressure, with diffusion accelerating once leading actors switch from defending the old standard to competing to define the new one.
matches.research_idea: Assemble a bond-level dataset of New York- and English-law sovereign issuances and test whether crisis shocks, issuer/underwriter prominence, and public-sector advocacy predict adoption and specific parameter choices of CACs and related terms over time.

matches.theme_name: Do contractual devices (insurance, covenants, staged payments, MAC/force-majeure language) adequately allocate risk for large, systemic shocks, or is public intervention required?
matches.specific_contribution: In the sovereign bond market, successive crises (Mexico 1995, Asia 1997–98, Argentina 2001) triggered movement from unanimity clauses to collective-action clauses, and vocal public-sector pressure was pivotal in reaching the tipping point at which leading market participants embraced and refined the restructuring-friendly standard.
matches.generalized_contribution: Systemic shocks can catalyze the uptake of contractual mechanisms for coordinated restructuring, and broad diffusion may depend on complementary public-sector advocacy.
matches.research_idea: Using panel data on sovereign bond terms and timelines of crises and public-sector initiatives, estimate whether external policy advocacy accelerates post-crisis adoption of restructuring-enabling clauses beyond what shocks alone explain.

matches.theme_name: What are the trade-offs between standardized boilerplate and bespoke drafting for transaction costs, liquidity, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: Documenting that boilerplate in sovereign bonds shifts mainly through industry-wide changes following major shocks—while individualized changes arise from significant issuer-specific events—the study indicates standardized templates, rather than bespoke drafting, dominate meaningful contract evolution in this market.
matches.generalized_contribution: In sophisticated debt markets, major contractual revisions tend to occur via standardized, industry-wide updates triggered by shocks, with bespoke deviations playing a limited, event-driven role.
matches.research_idea: Compile a time-series corpus of sovereign bond contracts to test whether industry-wide shocks predict standardized revisions while issuer-specific shocks yield bespoke tweaks, and assess how frequently each mode of change occurs.

matches.theme_name: Can contract clauses be designed to allocate macro- or systemic-shock risk (pandemics, exchange controls, MAE/MAC events) effectively without creating excessive moral hazard or perverse incentives?
matches.specific_contribution: Focusing on sovereign bonds, the article shows that large shocks were followed by adoption of CACs and subsequent innovations like aggregation clauses that increased the feasibility of coordinated restructurings across instruments.
matches.generalized_contribution: After major shocks, markets adopt voting and aggregation mechanisms that facilitate coordinated adjustments to allocate restructuring risk across holders and instruments.
matches.research_idea: Examine whether the incidence and specific design of voting and aggregation clauses increase following macro-crisis events by coding sovereign bond terms over time and relating adoption patterns to crisis timelines.

matches.theme_name: Which institutional or doctrinal reforms (statutory sovereign bankruptcy, coordinated creditor fora, harmonized conflict-of-laws rules) are feasible and likely to improve restructuring speed, predictability, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a sovereign bond dataset, the study documents that New York-law bonds shifted from unanimity action clauses to collective action clauses after crisis shocks and public-sector pressure, a change that significantly increased the ability to conduct restructurings.
matches.generalized_contribution: Adopting collective action clauses in sovereign bonds increases restructuring capacity and can be catalyzed by external policy pressure.
matches.research_idea: Quantify how adoption of collective action clauses affects restructuring speed and predictability by assembling issuance- and outcome-level data before and after policy-driven adoption waves across governing-law regimes.

matches.specific_contribution: Analyzing a longitudinal dataset of sovereign bonds under New York and English law, the study finds that boilerplate innovations diffuse through clustered, shock-induced experimentation, reach a tipping point where leading participants switch to the new standard, and then follow an S-curve of adoption culminating in market-wide standardization (e.g., Mexico’s 2003 CAC model).

matches.research_idea: Estimate the effect of crisis episodes and policy interventions on the probability of collective action clause inclusion in sovereign bonds, controlling for issuer characteristics and investor composition.

matches.specific_contribution: Using a dataset of New York-law sovereign bonds, the study documents the industry-wide shift from unanimity action clauses to collective action clauses—along with related terms like aggregation—triggered by crisis shocks and public-sector pressure, a change that significantly increased the ability of bondholders and issuers to execute restructurings.

matches.specific_contribution: Public-sector pressure helped trigger the tipping point toward CAC adoption, while subsequent CAC-related innovations were driven by top private market participants competing to shape the new standard.

matches.specific_contribution: In New York-law sovereign bonds, replacing unanimity clauses with CACs materially increased bondholders' and issuers' ability to execute restructurings, marking a watershed in covenant design.

papers.title: ARTICLE: Stickiness and Incomplete Contracts
papers.abstract:
In the 1990s, Sprint PCS, one of the leading telecommunications companies in the United States, created a wireless affiliate program. Under the affiliate program, Sprint and its partners would conclude several agreementsthat established cooperation between the parties. Under the terms of these agreements, the affiliates would invest "hundreds of millions of dollars" in orderto offer services on behalf of Sprint under the Sprint name.In return, a noncompete clause stipulated that the affiliates would be the exclusive providers of Sprint services in their regions covered by the affiliate program.
On December 15, 2004, Sprint announced a planned merger with Nextel Communications, Inc., then the fifth-leading provider in the U.S. mobile phone industry. Nextel operated stores and offered services in many parts of the United States, including regions covered by Sprint's affiliate program. After the merger, Nextel's services would be rebranded under the Sprint name. The affiliates did not look favorably upon the planned merger. They alleged that the rebranding of the Nextel stores and services would cause the newly formed Sprint Nextel to directly compete against them in their service areas, thus violating the noncompete provision. Consequently, they filed for an injunction seeking to prevent the merger, alleging a breach of contract.
Conspicuously, however, while the agreements that Sprint concluded with its partners under the affiliate program included a choice-of-law clause determining the substantive law applicable in the dispute, none of them included a choice-of-forum provision that would determine where the partners could sue.To Sprint, this omission would become detrimental.
In 2005, the affiliates commenced parallel suits in both Delawareand Illinois.In 2008, in the context of a separate dispute regarding the acquisition of Clearwire Corporation by Sprint, they pursued a similar strategy.
In an effort to minimize the harm resulting from this multi-forum litigation, Sprint negotiated a forbearance agreement, inwhich the parties promised to limit their claims to the jurisdictions in which their respective lawsuits were currently pending and to coordinate discovery in the parallel suits in order to reduce costs.In addition, the parties amended their existing agreements to include a choice-of-forum provision.With its less adversarial affiliates, Sprint negotiated exclusive choice-of-forum provisions that would limit its exposure in the future.However, notwithstanding these attempts, the subsequent proceedings were so complex and costly that Sprint Nextel ultimately resolved the lawsuits by buying eight out of its ten affiliates. The largest of these transactions was the $ 4.3 billion acquisition of Alamosa Holdings in February 2006.
The Sprint-Nextel merger provides a particularly striking example of the profound negative consequences that it can have to leave important terms in a contract unspecified. And yet, contractual gaps such as these are no exception in even the highestvalue transactions between the most sophisticated actors. For instance, choice-of-forum provisions are similarly absent in the May 2011 underwriting agreement between Merrill Lynch (represented by Cahill Gordon & Reindel LLP) and Celanese Corp. for $ 140 million,and the November 2015 common unit purchase agreement between Sunoco (represented by Latham & Watkins LLP) and Energy Transfer Equity for $ 64.5 million.Indeed, a systematic study of half a million "material" contracts reported to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) between 2000 and 2016 reveals that dispute settlement provisions are absent in more than half of all agreements.
To students of contract law, this variation in the adoption of dispute settlement provisions presents an intriguing puzzle. Wecurrently lack any theory that would predict parties to prefer the uncertainties associated with not having a dispute resolution clause over the predictability that comes with choosing a forum ex ante. And even if we could conceive of such a theory ex post facto, it would need to explain not only the existence of contractual gaps with respect to the forum, but also the great variation between different contracts. It is difficult to find consistency in the use of dispute settlement provisions across any coherent dimension that is often thought to induce homogeneity, such as the type of the underlying transaction or the industry. Indeed, even multiple contracts of the same company vary widely in their use of dispute resolution clauses, such that any given company sometimes includes them and sometimes does not.
But if the explanation is neither the identity of the party nor the characteristics of the deal, what does explain the observed variation in contractual terms? To get an anecdotal taste of the empirical argument advanced in this Article, consider the case of Huron Consulting Group Inc., a leading provider of financial services. On July 31, 2007, Huron announced the acquisition of Callaway Partners, LLC. Callaway specializes in finance and accounting project management. The purchase price was $ 60 million, paid in cash.Then, on January 4, 2007, Huron announced the acquisition of Wellspring Partners LTD for $ 65 million.On the same day, Huron also announced it had entered into a definitive merger agreement to acquire Glass & Associates, Inc., a leading turnaround and restructuring firm, for $ 30 million.What is striking about these acquisitions is that, while the underlying contracts for all of them include a choice-of-law clause specifying the "internal laws of the State of Illinois" as the governing law,none of them include a dispute settlement provision.
In searching for consistency among the three transactions that may help explain this absence, a glance at the underlying agreements--as filed with the SEC--is instructive. What can benoticed is that all three contracts use the same font and format, and have similarly titled provisions.For instance, the substantive choice-of-law provision in all three contracts is titled "Applicable Law,"which is a rarity among these agreements. Indeed, the three agreements look like almost identical copies of one another. A study of the notice clause reveals who wrote these contracts. All acquired parties were represented by different sophisticated and successful law firms, namely Epstein, Becker & Green, P.C.; Kirkpatrick & Lockhart Nicholson Graham LLP (now K&L Gates LLP); and McDermott Will & Emery LLP. At the same time, what all three agreements have in common is the counsel representing Huron, an experienced partner of one of the largest law firms in the United States. Together, this suggests that all agreements were written based on the same template, provided by the acquirer's counsel. This template, in turn, did not include a dispute settlement clause, and so neither did any of the agreements supporting the acquisitions.
At its core, this Article is a systematic and comprehensive investigation of what is exemplified by the case of Huron. It shows that the decision whether to include a dispute settlement provision is not typically made in an effort to maximize the joint surplus of the agreement. Instead, the presence of these clauses is almost exclusively driven by the lawyers that are hired to draft the contract between the parties. And even though most of the transactions under investigation have a value of several million--or even billion--dollars, the dynamics of the deal seem not to explain the lawyers' decision to include or not include a dispute settlement clause. Instead, external counsel relies heavily on templates, and whether the final contract addresses the settlement of disputes is determined almost exclusively by the template that a law firm uses.
Exploiting the fact that some law firms collapsed during the period of observation, forcing lawyers to move to different firms and clients to seek new counsel, this Article further demonstrates that there is no evidence to suggest that companies strategically hire law firms that use the most beneficial template for theirdeals. Similarly, external variation in the default rules on forum choice seems to have no bearing on how parties approach issues of forum selection. Instead, the final contract is almost always identical to the first draft that was provided by one of the law firms. In contrast, the historical practice of the law firm receiving the first draft has no measurable bearing on whether the final contract specifies a forum. This suggests that external counsel virtually never bargains over or adapts dispute settlement clauses as found in the initial draft.
The results show that sticky drafting practices characterize the most fundamental aspects of commercial transactions across a wide range of contexts. In doing so, these results contribute to the literature on the economics of contract design and the role of the legal profession in several important ways.
First, much of modern legal and economic scholarship on contracts assumes that sophisticated parties routinely write optimal agreements. Meanwhile, the popular Coase Theorem teaches us that default rules do not matter if transaction costs are negligible, because parties would simply contract around inefficient default rules.Together, these assumptions have resulted in a lethargy with respect to academic, regulatory, and judicial interest in analyzing and optimizing the default rules that pertain to transactions between sophisticated commercial actors.
The jurisprudence on the default rules of personal jurisdiction are a case in point. Over the past decade, the Supreme Courthas made important innovations in the legal framework surrounding dispute settlement provisions for claims directed against corporations.However, this jurisprudence was developed almost exclusively in the context of tort law and consumer contracts.At the same time, and consistent with the view that sophisticated actors are able to optimize the rules themselves, the Court has done very little to promote clarity in the at times opaque default rules on forum choice in contract disputes at arm's length. The results of this study lay bare an important practical limitation of theoretical approaches to these traditional accounts of contract design. Default rules such as those on forum choice can have important welfare implications because they affect not only the distribution, but also the final allocation of the contractual surplus. As such, it is worth spending scholarly, regulatory, and judicial attention to the design of efficient default rules even as they pertain to transactions between highly sophisticated actors.
Second, while the recent trend toward more empirical scholarship on contracts resulted in many valuable insights, one can observe a tendency for researchers to infer the efficiency of a clause from its prevalence in contracts between commercial actors. For instance, a desire to explain a seemingly incoherent set of contract terms has led to increasingly complex theoretical models explaining the interplay between formal and relational contracts.Only few have taken into consideration that the nuanced provisions in these contracts may not be optimized.The results of the study described in this Article suggest that it may be suitable to exert caution more frequently, thus determining efficiency on its own terms rather than to infer it from observed practice.
Third, this Article adds to and expands on the growing body of literature that emphasizes the significance of the law firm's role in the allocation of contractual rights. Prior research has found that the law firm is an important actor in explaining the design ofpari passuclauses in sovereign bond agreements,the prevalence of arbitration provisions in these contracts,exclusive forum provisions in corporate charters and bylaws,takeover defenses,and the language of S-1 statements filed in the course of initial or secondary public offerings.However, law firms do not seem to matter for the formulation of event risk covenants in corporate bonds when controlling for the underwriter.The study described in this Article is the first to investigate the influence of the law firm in a wide array of contractual relationships at arm's length, overcoming the problem of a lack of generalizability that affects previous contributions. It is also the first Article to compare the law firm's influence to that of the company by considering another important legal actor, the general counsel.
Finally, heterogeneity in contractual drafting practices suggests an important domain in which legal education can be value enhancing. In particular, by raising awareness of and advising their students on the pitfalls of template-driven contract drafting, law schools can enable students to significantly improve the distribution of contractual rights in favor of their clients.
This Article proceeds in seven parts. Part I offers a brief primer on the laws surrounding forum choice and dispute settlementclauses. Part II describes two theoretical approaches to the study of contract design and develops competing predictions on how contracts should be drafted. Part III introduces the data set and presents summary statistics. Part IV investigates whether the contracts in the data set reflect law firm or company preferences. Part V asks whether law firms ever bargain over the issue of forum choice. Part VI analyzes how resistant law firm templates are to changing circumstances in the legal environment. Finally, Part VII discusses limitations and the implications of the findings for the study and design of contracts.

matches.theme_name: Do standardized contract forms and drafting defaults systematically shape non-price deal terms and bargaining outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a corpus of roughly half a million SEC-filed material contracts from 2000–2016 and natural experiments from law firm collapses and lawyer/client moves, the study shows that inclusion of dispute-settlement clauses is driven almost entirely by the drafting law firm’s template and the first draft, with little evidence that bargaining or deal characteristics shape the term.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized templates and initial drafting defaults supplied by law firms strongly determine non-price deal terms and the allocation of dispute-resolution rights, largely independent of party identity or deal context.
matches.research_idea: Assemble a large corpus of contracts and exploit exogenous shifts in counsel (such as law firm collapses and lateral moves) to test whether initial law-firm templates, rather than party or deal characteristics, causally determine inclusion of dispute-resolution terms.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: By documenting that law firm templates and first drafts—rather than party optimization or shifting legal defaults—determine whether contracts include dispute-settlement clauses, and that lawyers rarely bargain over these terms, the study explains the persistence of potentially suboptimal boilerplate.
matches.generalized_contribution: Template dependence, minimal bargaining, and insensitivity to legal-environment changes perpetuate boilerplate clauses despite potential inefficiencies.
matches.research_idea: Investigate whether reliance on law-firm templates and limited negotiation over boilerplate sustains suboptimal clause language across deals, using contract text fingerprints and variation from firm dissolutions to identify path dependence.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do judicial interpretations of boilerplate contractual language shape market practice and subsequent contract drafting?
matches.specific_contribution: Analyzing external variation in forum-choice default rules, the study finds no measurable effect on whether sophisticated parties include forum-selection clauses.
matches.generalized_contribution: Judicial and doctrinal changes in forum-choice defaults do not reliably alter sophisticated parties’ adoption of forum-selection clauses.
matches.research_idea: Measure changes in adoption of forum-selection clauses before and after shifts in forum-choice default rules, using contract data and jurisdiction-specific legal shocks to identify effects.

matches.theme_name: Do professional intermediaries (law firms, underwriters, trustees, advisors) introduce agency costs that bias contract design and risk allocation?
matches.specific_contribution: Using SEC contract data and shocks from law-firm collapses that reassign lawyers and clients, the study shows external counsel’s templates almost entirely determine inclusion of dispute-settlement clauses, with no evidence that companies strategically hire for template advantages and little evidence of opposing counsel negotiating the term.
matches.generalized_contribution: Professional intermediaries—especially law firms—introduce agency-driven drafting inertia that biases contract design and risk allocation toward their templates rather than client-optimized terms.
matches.research_idea: Exploit exogenous changes in counsel identity (firm dissolutions, lateral partner moves) to test whether law-firm identity causally drives key non-price terms and whether clients strategically select counsel to avoid template-driven biases.

matches.theme_name: To what degree does forum-shopping and strategic exploitation of legal uncertainty alter creditor litigation strategies and restructuring outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The Sprint–Nextel example shows that omitting a forum-selection clause enabled affiliates to file parallel suits in multiple jurisdictions, increasing complexity and costs and contributing to buyouts of affiliates.
matches.generalized_contribution: Leaving dispute-resolution terms unspecified can facilitate forum-shopping, fragment litigation across courts, and increase dispute costs.
matches.research_idea: Test whether contracts lacking forum-selection clauses are associated with higher rates of multi-forum litigation and costlier dispute resolution than contracts with designated forums, using matched samples of corporate disputes.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do standardized boilerplate clauses (e.g., pari passu, governing-law, indemnities) generate systemic litigation externalities and market-wide vulnerabilities?
matches.specific_contribution: The Sprint–Nextel disputes illustrate how omission of a forum-selection clause enabled costly multi-forum litigation, and the study’s SEC corpus shows that more than half of material contracts similarly omit dispute-settlement terms due to sticky law-firm templates.
matches.generalized_contribution: Template-driven omission of dispute-resolution provisions can facilitate fragmented litigation and higher dispute costs across deals.
matches.research_idea: Link a large SEC contract corpus to litigation dockets to test whether template-driven omission of forum clauses correlates with greater multi-forum filings, longer case duration, and higher settlement costs.

matches.theme_name: Can empirical contract-level datasets reveal patterns of clause prevalence and evolution that should inform doctrinal or regulatory reform?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a half-million SEC-reported contracts from 2000–2016 and leveraging law-firm collapses and shifts in forum-choice defaults, the study maps the prevalence and determinants of dispute-settlement clauses and shows their resistance to legal-environment changes, motivating attention to default-rule design.
matches.generalized_contribution: Large contract-level datasets can reveal entrenched template effects, non-responsiveness to doctrinal shifts, and gaps between law and practice that inform doctrinal and regulatory reform.
matches.research_idea: Assemble a large corpus of material contracts and test whether clause prevalence and responsiveness to doctrinal changes vary with law-firm identity and lawyer mobility, then translate detected patterns into targeted default-rule reforms.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do legal ambiguities and doctrinal vagueness (e.g., in 'pari passu', 'loan' definitions, or damages measures) cause litigation, market uncertainty, and suboptimal contracting outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: Because sophisticated parties in the dataset rarely bargain over forum-choice terms and often leave them to defaults, opacity in forum-choice doctrine can materially shape dispute resolution outcomes.
matches.generalized_contribution: When parties do not contract around defaults, doctrinal vagueness in forum-choice rules can increase uncertainty and dispute costs.
matches.research_idea: Measure whether greater ambiguity in jurisdiction and forum-choice doctrines predicts higher litigation costs or forum-splitting in contracts that omit forum-selection clauses, using matched contract–case data.

matches.theme_name: What can large-scale, contract-by-contract textual and empirical analyses reveal about the gap between drafted language and actual functional allocations of risk?
matches.specific_contribution: Analyzing hundreds of thousands of contracts, the study shows that inclusion of dispute-resolution clauses tracks law-firm templates rather than deal features or party preferences, indicating the contract text may not mirror functional risk allocation.
matches.generalized_contribution: Corpus-based analyses can uncover misalignment between template-driven contract wording and economically intended allocations of risk and rights.
matches.research_idea: Conduct a contract-by-contract textual study to test whether template-driven clause usage diverges from transaction characteristics and observed dispute outcomes, indicating a gap between text and functional allocation.

matches.theme_name: What role do lawyers, underwriters, and other intermediaries play in creating, diffusing, and entrenching contractual innovations and standard clauses?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a 2000–2016 SEC contract corpus and natural experiments from law-firm collapses and lawyer/client moves, the study shows that law-firm templates and first-draft control almost entirely determine whether dispute-resolution clauses appear, with little role for companies’ general counsel or shifts in legal defaults.
matches.generalized_contribution: Intermediary law firms, via templates and control of initial drafts, create, diffuse, and entrench standard terms across contractual markets.
matches.research_idea: Estimate causal template effects by tracking clause adoption at the law-firm level over time and around lawyer mobility and firm-collapse events using a large contract corpus.

matches.theme_name: Do lawyers, deal teams, and legal intermediaries (as repeat players) add measurable economic value through drafting and structuring beyond mere documentation?
matches.specific_contribution: Findings that external counsel default to templates, rarely bargain, and do not tailor dispute-resolution clauses to deal characteristics suggest limited drafting value-add by repeat-player intermediaries in this domain.
matches.generalized_contribution: When template inertia dominates, repeat-player legal intermediaries may not add measurable economic value through tailored allocation of dispute-related risks.
matches.research_idea: Compare dispute incidence, costs, and outcomes for matched deals drafted by template-heavy versus customization-oriented law firms to assess whether intermediary drafting practices add economic value.
