In light of the conventional wisdom in law-and-economics, Ben-Shahar and White remarked that "given the enormous stakes, we expected that economic power would be used to dictate low prices, not selfish boilerplate."They speculated that the variation and the potential inefficiency were due to internal agency conflicts within the parties, but conceded that they did not "offer a satisfactory explanation for the variance of terms across the different [original equipment manufacturer("OEM")] contracts, or for the conjecture that some of these terms are inefficient."
The puzzle that Ben-Shahar and White raise is echoed repeatedly by practitioners and commentators in the business and legal press, who invoke bargaining power to explain both static and dynamic observations of contracting patterns. One static observation is that business entities that dominate their industries tend to adopt different contractual allocations of similar risks depending on whether they are buyers or sellers. When they are buyers or licensees, they demand extensive warranties and indemnification promises from their counterparts; when they are sellers or licensors, they disclaim, limit remedies, and demand indemnification from their customers. A dynamic observation is that contract terms such as covenants in loan and debt agreements, or material adverse change ("MAC") clauses in mergers and acquisitions agreements, fluctuate over time between "buyer-friendly" and "seller-friendly" versions as market conditions change.
The set of questions addressing when and why bargaining or market power is a determinant of nonprice terms remains unexplored and worthy of investigation. The conventional law-and-economics theory offers a starting point for this analysis by offering two irrelevance propositions: (1) bargaining power affects the price but not the nonprice terms of a contract (the strong-form version); and (2) the allocation of bargaining power may lead to different nonprice terms but does not change the likelihood that the parties will agree to efficient terms (the weak-form version).Each of these propositions depends on a set of implicit assumptions, including perfect information and zero transactions costs. We relax these assumptions in this Article to bridge theory and practice, by providing a theoretical framework to understand when and how bargaining power determines contract design. To focus on bargaining power, we assume that each party can read and understand all provisions in their contract and set aside important effects that stem from lack of sophistication or bounded rationality.
The strong-form irrelevance proposition treats a price term as purely distributional: it allocates the surplus and has no effect on size. However, variations in price terms can change the optimal nonprice terms when there is a change in price. We give two instances of this phenomenon. First, a different price alters one (or both) party's rate of substitution between price and nonprice terms. For example, a business executive who is richly paid may be willing to sacrifice a greater amount in salary for an official title than one who is less well paid. Second, a higher or lower price determines the severity of the adverse-selection or moral-hazard problems. For example, we would expect a loan agreement to have tighter and more extensive covenants to address these problems when the market rate of interest is high than when it is low, all else equal.
Turning to the weak-form proposition, we outline four ways in which the shift in the bargaining power might lead to a deviation from efficient contract design. First, the pursuit of advantage in negotiations exacerbates the inclination of negotiators to engage in value-claiming rather than value-creating strategies. Second, the party with greater bargaining power has better incentives to invest effort and resources in innovating and developing contractual opportunities to create value. Third, business contracting often occurs in a two-stage process: the price and other important terms are decided by the business principals, and the design "details" are delegated to their respective lawyers. The exercise of bargaining power in the second stage, after price has been determined, may distort the agreement on nonprice terms. Fourth, in negotiations characterized by information asymmetry, unequal bargaining power might encourageexcessive signaling or screening activity in the design of nonprice terms.
Each of these effects warrants more detailed treatment and we analyze only one of them in this Article. We examine the impact of unequal bargaining power when markets have buyers with heterogeneous valuations of alternative contract terms and these values are not observable by the seller(s).Building on insights from the economics of industrial organization, we demonstrate theoretically that one-sided bargaining power can lead to the inefficient use of nonprice terms to screen or signal (depending on whether the power lies with the seller or the buyer, respectively). We show that a monopolist or otherwise dominant seller may screen by offering suboptimal contract quality to the buyer who values quality less. At the other extreme, when the buyer has all the bargaining power, similar to the case of perfect competition, the buyer who values the nonprice term less will seek to avoid subsidizing other buyer types by agreeing to suboptimal nonprice terms, to signal her type to the sellers.
To illustrate, consider a market for automobiles in which sellers can agree to either limited or extended warranties and in which buyers have different valuations of the warranty provisions because they are either careful or careless drivers. The seller cannot observe which drivers are careful or careless. Suppose that both groups of buyers would pay more for the extended warranty than it would cost the seller to provide, and the extended warranty is therefore efficient. A monopolist would seek to maximize its share of the surplus in each sale by offering both extended and limited warranties at prices that would induce the careful driver to purchase a limited warranty. Similar inefficient separation would occur in a perfectly competitive market. If sellers offered the extended warranty to all buyers at a single price, careful drivers would subsidize the careless drivers. The careful drivers, then, would have an incentive to choose the limited warranty so as to signal their type to the market andreceive a price reduction that exceeds the value of the foregone warranty.
The problem of extreme allocations of bargaining power in either direction stems, in part, from the fact that one party has the power to dictate the terms of trade. The party with this power is willing, in many circumstances, to sacrifice some of the aggregate surplus in order to capture a larger share of the surplus. Therefore, a more "even" sharing of the surplus may address these inefficiencies in contract design. The circumstances that would balance bargaining power in this manner, however, are not obvious. After all, competitive markets essentially allocate all the power to the buyers without leaving any surplus for the sellers. We suggest three ways of representing more "even" sharing of bargaining power. In the first, some competition is introduced by allowing another seller (an entrant) to compete with an existing seller (an incumbent). In the second, the power of commitment is reduced by letting the contracting parties renegotiate the original contract. In the third, the seller's power to dictate the terms is curtailed by allowing the buyer to dictate the terms with some delay. In each of these cases, we demonstrate the key result that the conditions mitigate or eliminate the inefficiencies of screening and signaling through nonprice terms.
The Article is organized as follows. Part I investigates various meanings for unequal bargaining power. Part II states the weak and strong forms of the bargaining power irrelevance propositions, and then outlines various paths by which bargaining power might determine contract design. Part III reviews related literature in industrial organization concerning how monopoly and perfect competition can distort the quality of goods provided. Part IV provides a more detailed analysis of the effect of unequal bargaining power on contract design when parties are asymmetricallyinformed as to the value and cost of a given nonprice term. Part V shows that more even bargaining power can attenuate inefficient screening and signaling through nonprice terms. Despite the inefficiencies caused by unequal bargaining power, we suggest briefly in Part VI that legal institutions are unlikely to be able to mitigate these problems by constraining the parties' freedom of contract. We conclude with a comment as to possible directions for future research.

matches.theme_name: How do bargaining power asymmetries and repeat-player advantages shape non-price contract terms and the distribution of surplus in sovereign and major corporate transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a formal screening/signaling framework under asymmetric information that relaxes perfect-information and zero-transaction-cost assumptions, the paper shows that unequal bargaining power drives one-sided nonprice terms (e.g., warranties, termination rights, forum clauses), reallocating and sometimes shrinking surplus, while entry, renegotiation, or delayed buyer dictation can mitigate these inefficiencies.
matches.generalized_contribution: Unequal bargaining power determines nonprice contract design and can reduce total surplus through inefficient screening or signaling, whereas mechanisms that balance power can restore efficiency.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model of contract design with asymmetric information in which one party wields bargaining power, characterize the resulting nonprice terms and surplus allocation, and analyze how entry, renegotiation, or delayed buyer dictation attenuate distortions.

matches.theme_name: To what degree do contract design choices (termination rights, MAC/MAC clauses, break fees) allocate completion risk in mergers and acquisitions, and how do they affect bargaining dynamics under asymmetric power?
matches.specific_contribution: The introduction notes practitioner claims that acquirer dominance leads to broad termination rights and that MAC terms swing with market conditions, and the theory advanced implies that unequal bargaining power can distort such nonprice provisions that allocate completion risk.
matches.generalized_contribution: In M&A, shifts in bargaining power can influence termination and MAC provisions that allocate completion risk, potentially producing inefficient clause design.
matches.research_idea: Formally model how bargaining-power asymmetries in mergers affect the optimal design of termination and MAC provisions that allocate completion risk.

matches.theme_name: How do market conditions, bargaining power, and counterparty composition drive adoption and specific wording of non-price clauses (MAE/MAC, covenants, break fees) in M&A and lending contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: By showing that price changes can alter optimal nonprice terms, the paper predicts, for example, that higher market interest rates tighten covenants in lending agreements and that MAC provisions in M&A swing with market conditions as bargaining leverage shifts.
matches.generalized_contribution: Market conditions and relative bargaining power help determine the adoption and stringency of nonprice clauses in lending and M&A contracts.
matches.research_idea: Construct a formal model linking market interest rates and bargaining leverage to the choice and tightness of covenants and MAC clauses in lending and M&A under adverse selection and moral hazard.

matches.theme_name: How do market conditions and relative bargaining power among actors determine debt terms, restructuring allocations, and recovery outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: As an application of its price–nonprice linkage, the paper predicts that when market interest rates are high, loan agreements will feature tighter and more extensive covenants to address more severe adverse selection and moral hazard.
matches.generalized_contribution: Higher market interest rates are associated with tighter debt covenants because they heighten adverse selection and moral hazard concerns.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal lending model in which changes in the interest rate endogenously shift covenant tightness by altering adverse selection and moral hazard incentives.

matches.theme_name: Can clearer, mandatory contractual defaults (e.g., standard voting rules, enforcement waivers) improve predictability without producing adverse distributional or moral-hazard effects?
matches.specific_contribution: The introduction states that legal institutions are unlikely to mitigate bargaining-power-induced distortions by constraining freedom of contract, casting doubt on the efficacy of mandatory terms to improve outcomes.
matches.generalized_contribution: Mandatory contractual constraints are unlikely to reliably improve efficiency in the presence of bargaining-power distortions.
matches.research_idea: Build a formal model to assess whether imposing mandatory defaults improves efficiency when unequal bargaining power and asymmetric information drive distortions in nonprice terms.

matches.theme_name: Do lawyers, deal teams, and legal intermediaries (as repeat players) add measurable economic value through drafting and structuring beyond mere documentation?
matches.specific_contribution: The article identifies a two-stage contracting process in which principals set price and lawyers later draft design details, and posits that exercising bargaining power in this second stage can distort nonprice terms away from efficiency.
matches.generalized_contribution: Delegating post-price drafting to lawyers enables bargaining power to be channeled into nonprice terms, potentially distorting contract design and reducing efficiency.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model of two-stage contracting in which principals choose price and delegated lawyers draft nonprice terms, to assess how post-price bargaining power affects the efficiency of contract design.

matches.theme_name: Does enforceability of exculpatory or limitation-of-liability clauses in consumer, broker, and financial contracts protect market activity or undermine accountability and market integrity?
matches.specific_contribution: The article briefly suggests that legal institutions are unlikely to mitigate bargaining-power-driven inefficiencies in nonprice terms by constraining freedom of contract, casting doubt on the efficacy of policing one-sided clauses such as disclaimers and limitations.
matches.generalized_contribution: Limiting the enforceability of one-sided nonprice terms is unlikely to reliably improve efficiency when asymmetric information and bargaining power drive contract design choices.
matches.research_idea: Construct a formal model of bargaining over nonprice terms under asymmetric information to evaluate whether legal constraints on exculpatory and limitation-of-liability clauses enhance or diminish surplus relative to freedom of contract.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries-adverse selection and moral hazard-shape the design of contractual devices (collateral, covenants, disclosure) in sovereign and corporate lending?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a formal asymmetric-information model of contract design, the paper shows that unequal bargaining power induces parties to use nonprice terms for screening or signaling in ways that can be inefficient, and it specifically predicts in lending contexts that higher interest rates (which intensify adverse selection and moral hazard) lead to tighter, more extensive covenants.
matches.generalized_contribution: Information asymmetries shape the adoption and stringency of contractual devices such as covenants and collateral, with market prices and bargaining-power allocations determining whether these tools are efficient or distortive.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model of sovereign and corporate lending with adverse selection and moral hazard in which interest rates and bargaining-power allocations endogenously determine covenant and collateral design, and characterize how shifts in these parameters alter the efficiency of the resulting terms.

matches.theme_name: Do material adverse effect/change (MAE/MAC) clauses operate primarily as true risk-allocation devices or as strategic deal-termination levers in M&A transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: Via a formal screening/signaling framework under asymmetric information, the article explains that shifts in bargaining power can lead parties to deploy nonprice terms—illustrated by practitioners’ observations of MAC clauses swinging between buyer- and seller-friendly variants—as strategic levers that may produce inefficient designs rather than purely allocate risk.
matches.generalized_contribution: Unequal bargaining power under asymmetric information can make clauses like MAC provisions function as strategic bargaining instruments whose content tracks leverage rather than solely underlying risk allocation, sometimes at the cost of efficiency.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model of M&A negotiations with asymmetric information to analyze whether shifts in relative bargaining power cause MAC clauses to alternate between risk-allocation and strategic termination roles and to identify when such designs are inefficient.

papers.node_id: 1988uilllrev519!!ARTICLE: THE ACT OF STATE DOCTRINE IN CONTRACT CASES AS A CONFLICT-OF-LAWS RULE 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE ACT OF STATE DOCTRINE IN CONTRACT CASES AS A CONFLICT-OF-LAWS RULE 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
papers.abstract:
Courts have recently begun to apply the act of state doctrine in cases in which a foreign obligor claims that a foreign act of state modifies the contractual obligation owed to a U.S. obligee.Allied Bank International v. Banco Credito Agricola de Cartagois the best known case in this category. For some time courts have encountered a second category of cases involving the performance of contracts.  In these cases a party claims that the foreign act of state modified the contractual obligation of a U.S. obligor owed to a foreign obligee.Alfred Dunhill of London, Inc. v. Republic of Cubamay serve as an example.  In some of these performance of contract cases the courts have held that the foreign act of state modified the contractual obligation; in others, courts have held to the contrary. In all these cases the central question was whether a commercial agreement that had contacts with both the United States and the foreign country was affected by a foreign law or decree promulgated after the contract had been entered into.
Professor Henkin has said that the act of state doctrine is a conflict-of-laws rule.This statement is undoubtedly correct because a rule dealing with the question whether a foreign law or the law of the forum applies to an agreement is a question of conflict of laws.Professor Henkin's statement has been repeated many times by courtsand commentators.Courts and commentators, however, have not analyzed the statement's meaning in connection with contract cases.  The question in these cases is whether and to what extent the act of state doctrine modifies the traditional conflict-of-laws rules applicable to contracts.
This article compares the results that courts have reached by applying or rejecting the act of state doctrine in cases involving performance of contract disputes with the results they would have reached by applying the traditional conflict-of-laws approaches.  The article demonstrates that the results reached in such cases under the act of state doctrine could also have been reached by applying traditional conflict-of-laws rules.  Consequently, the act of state doctrine as applied to contract cases is nothing but a new and fancy dress for old solutions.

matches.theme_name: Do judicial doctrines-such as act-of-state, sovereign immunity, and abstention/comity-unduly limit creditors' remedies in cross-border disputes and require doctrinal reform to balance politics and predictability?
matches.specific_contribution: Comparing contract-performance cases invoking or rejecting the act-of-state doctrine (including Allied Bank and Alfred Dunhill) with outcomes under traditional conflict-of-laws, the article shows that act-of-state adds no independent constraint on enforcement because courts could have reached the same results via ordinary conflicts rules.
matches.generalized_contribution: In cross-border contract disputes, applying the act-of-state doctrine does not materially change enforcement outcomes relative to traditional conflict-of-laws analysis.
matches.research_idea: Conduct a doctrinal comparison of cross-border contract cases that applied the act-of-state doctrine against counterfactual outcomes under traditional conflict-of-laws to assess whether act-of-state independently limits creditor enforcement and to evaluate the case for doctrinal reform.

matches.theme_name: When and on what grounds should domestic courts review or abstain from adjudicating claims arising from foreign sovereign acts (act-of-state and comity doctrines)?
matches.specific_contribution: By comparing outcomes in contract-performance disputes resolved with and without the act-of-state doctrine, the article shows that courts can resolve the applicable-law question—and thus adjudicate—using traditional conflict-of-laws without relying on act-of-state deference.
matches.generalized_contribution: In cross-border contract disputes involving foreign sovereign acts, abstention under the act-of-state doctrine is unnecessary because traditional conflict-of-laws methods suffice to decide which law governs.
matches.research_idea: Analyze case law in cross-border contract disputes involving foreign sovereign acts to determine when abstention under the act-of-state doctrine is superfluous by showing that traditional conflict-of-laws methods yield the same outcomes.

matches.theme_name: How do cross-border legal conflicts-choice-of-law, extraterritorial reach, and conflicting forum judgments-shape enforceability and predictability in international financial contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: Through a doctrinal comparison of act-of-state and traditional conflict-of-laws approaches in cross-border contract-performance cases involving post-contract foreign decrees, the article finds that the choice of doctrine does not change governing-law determinations or the enforceability of obligations.
matches.generalized_contribution: In international contract disputes, substituting the act-of-state doctrine for ordinary conflict-of-laws analysis does not alter governing-law outcomes or enforceability, indicating limited effect on predictability.
matches.research_idea: Compare outcomes in international contract disputes resolved under the act-of-state doctrine with counterfactual outcomes under traditional conflict-of-laws to assess whether doctrinal choice affects enforceability and predictability.

matches.theme_name: How do courts' use of emergency or adaptive doctrines in crises influence creditor protections and the enforceability of sovereign obligations?
matches.specific_contribution: By comparing outcomes in contract performance disputes involving foreign acts of state (e.g., Allied Bank and Dunhill) to those produced by traditional conflict-of-laws approaches, the article shows that invoking the act of state doctrine does not change the enforceability outcomes that courts would otherwise reach.
matches.generalized_contribution: Judicial reliance on foreign-relations doctrines like act of state in contract disputes involving sovereign acts does not, by itself, alter creditor protections or enforceability relative to standard conflict-of-laws analysis.
matches.research_idea: Conduct a doctrinal comparison of contract cases invoking the act of state doctrine against counterfactual outcomes under traditional conflict-of-laws rules to test whether crisis- or foreign-relations-driven doctrines materially affect the enforceability of obligations linked to sovereign acts.

matches.theme_name: How do cross-border regulatory measures (sanctions, capital controls, deposit freezes) alter contractual rights, remedies, and the incentives of creditors and debtors?
matches.specific_contribution: By comparing performance-of-contract cases such as Allied Bank and Alfred Dunhill, the article shows that outcomes attributed to foreign acts of state (post-contract decrees, exchange controls) when courts applied or rejected the act of state doctrine could equally have been reached via traditional conflict-of-laws rules, rendering the doctrine redundant in these disputes.
matches.generalized_contribution: In cross-border contract disputes, the effects of foreign sovereign regulatory measures on private contractual rights can be resolved under standard conflict-of-laws principles without reliance on a distinct act of state doctrine.
matches.research_idea: Undertake a doctrinal comparison of performance-of-contract cases in which foreign post-contract regulations purported to modify obligations, assessing whether outcomes differ when analyzed under the act of state doctrine versus traditional conflict-of-laws rules.
